1044.title: Rebecca Gratz
1044.hook: founded the first Jewish Sunday school in America in 1838
1044.howItsDone: Synagogues in America run weekend or after-school religious schools where volunteer and part-time teachers teach Hebrew, prayer, Bible, holidays and history, a model often traced to Rebecca Gratz's Hebrew Sunday School in Philadelphia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Grace Aguilar, and the line a woman's voice. Did you read a page by a woman writer? Today, one last woman for this stretch, a teacher across the ocean in Philadelphia. Day one thousand forty-four.

Sunday morning in Philadelphia. Church bells. Children in their best clothes walking to Sunday school with lesson books under their arms. And a few Jewish children watching them go, or walking along with their friends, because there is no Jewish school for them to go to. A woman named Rebecca Gratz notices, and asks herself a practical question. Why not a school for Jewish children, on the day they're free? In 1838, her answer gets its first class.
screen: `SUNDAY MORNING, PHILADELPHIA.` → `NO SCHOOL FOR JEWISH CHILDREN.` → `WHY NOT ONE OF OUR OWN?`

segments.voice: Rebecca Gratz was already busy. She came from a well-known Jewish family in Philadelphia, and she had spent years building things for people in need: a society to help orphans, a society of Jewish women to help poor Jewish families. She never married, and she helped raise her sister's children after their mother died. Then came the school. She called it the Hebrew Sunday School. The idea, a school on Sunday, was one her Christian neighbors were already using, and she saw no reason Jewish children couldn't have it too, filled with their own Bible, their own prayers, their own history. The teachers were young Jewish women, volunteers. They had few books, so they made do, and some of them wrote the lessons themselves. The children came. Behind it is a command the Torah gives to every parent, in the Shema itself: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way." Rebecca Gratz took that and asked: and when the parents can't, who will? The school answered: the community will. And it would be women who taught. Her model, a Jewish school on the weekend, run by the community, spread to other cities, and versions of it still exist in synagogues today. There's also a story people tell, that she was the model for the Jewish heroine Rebecca in Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe. Nobody has proven it. What can be shown is quieter: a woman, a free morning, and children who learned their own story.

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: teach a child something. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind a child in your life, your own, a relative, a neighbor, a student. Think of one thing you know that they don't yet: how to tie a knot, a word in another language, a family story, a blessing, why the moon changes shape. Keep it small. Picture the moment you'll tell them, where you'll be sitting, what they'll ask. If you pray, you can hold that child in your prayer. If not, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Rebecca Gratz. The Philadelphia woman who built help for orphans and the poor, and opened the Hebrew Sunday School so Jewish children could learn their own story. Today's word.
Your line: sunday school. Today, teach a child one small thing, on whatever day you have free. Day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: About fifteen million
1045.hook: Jews today live mostly in Israel and North America, with communities worldwide
1045.howItsDone: Some communities gathering a minyan avoid counting people by number, saying "not one, not two" or counting with the words of a verse; population estimates are made by demographers, who note that the answer depends on who is counted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebecca Gratz, and the line sunday school: a school on the day the children were free. Did you teach a child something? That closes the women's stretch. Today we turn to Jewish life now, and start by counting. Day one thousand forty-five.

Some prayers need a minyan, a quorum, and so someone at the door has to count heads. And in some synagogues, the person counting won't say one, two, three. Some say, not one, not two, not three. Some count by the words of a verse, one word per person. It sounds like a quirk. It's actually a very old instinct: be careful about counting people like objects. Keep that instinct in mind, because today's title is a number, and an enormous one. About fifteen million.
screen: `COUNTING FOR A MINYAN.` → `NOT ONE, NOT TWO.` → `A VERY OLD CAUTION.`

segments.voice: The caution goes back to the Torah. When Moses is told to take a census, each person gives half a shekel of silver, so that no plague comes among them. The rabbis read it this way: count the coins, not the heads. Later, when King David counts the people directly, the book of Samuel tells of a plague that follows. Behind both stories sits a conviction: a person is not a unit. And there's an older promise still. God takes Abraham outside at night and says: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." The point of that count is that you can't finish it. Now the modern number in today's title: about fifteen million Jews in the world. It is an estimate, not a head count, because counting Jews raises real questions. Who counts? Jewish movements answer differently. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism count a person Jewish through a Jewish mother or a conversion under Jewish law; Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism in North America also count a child of one Jewish parent who is raised Jewish. Some people with Jewish roots don't call themselves Jewish; some who do, others wouldn't count. So the number comes with an asterisk. Where do they live? Mostly in two places, Israel and North America. And then in communities around the world: France and Britain, Argentina and Brazil, Russia and Ukraine, South Africa, Australia, Morocco, India, and elsewhere, some large, some a handful of families with one old synagogue. The number is big and small at once. Big enough to fill cities. Small next to the stars. Each one of them a name, not a unit.
screen: `COUNT THE COINS, NOT THE HEADS.` · `COUNT THE STARS, IF YOU CAN.` · `WHO COUNTS? MOVEMENTS DIFFER.` · `ISRAEL, NORTH AMERICA, EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `FIFTEEN MILLION.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: count your own community, the old careful way. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind the people who make up your community: a congregation, a family, a team, the regulars at a café, a street. Don't count them with numbers. Instead, go one by one, and give each one a name, or a face, or one thing they do. Notice who comes easily and who you almost forgot. Keep going until you run out, or until the bell. That's a count where every one is a person. The bell holds the time.
Minyan. The quorum needed for some prayers, and the old instinct behind it: count the coins, not the heads, a care that holds even for the fifteen million Jews alive today. Today's word.
Your line: fifteen million. Today, when you hear a big number about people, picture one face inside it. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: Jews by choice
1046.hook: converts, like Ruth, are fully Jewish; reminding them of their past is forbidden
1046.howItsDone: Conversion to Judaism involves study with a rabbi and usually appearing before a rabbinic court, and often immersion in a mikveh; movements differ in their requirements, and Jewish law forbids reminding a convert of their past.

segments.voice: Yesterday, minyan, and your line was fifteen million: a big number, counted with care, one face at a time. Did you picture a face inside a number? Today, some of those faces arrived by choosing. Day one thousand forty-six.

A dusty road out of Moab. Three widows walking. The oldest, Naomi, is going home to Bethlehem, and she turns to her two daughters-in-law and tells them to go back to their own mothers. One of them, Orpah, kisses her and goes, and the text doesn't blame her. The other, Ruth, holds on, and tells her: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Today is about people who say that sentence with their lives.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `ORPAH GOES HOME.` → `RUTH HOLDS ON.`

segments.voice: Jewish tradition reads Ruth as a convert, someone not born Jewish who chose to join the people and its God. Hebrew has a phrase for such a person: ger tzedek, a righteous convert. The word ger in the Torah means a stranger, someone who lives among you. The Torah is firm about the stranger: "The stranger that sojourneth with you shall be unto you as the home-born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The rabbis read that verse, among others, about converts. And the Mishnah sets down a rule about words that wound: to someone from a family of converts, you may not say, remember what your ancestors did. You don't bring up their past. You don't make them a guest in their own house. In Jewish law, once someone has converted, they are fully Jewish. Not almost. Not Jewish with a footnote. When a convert asked the medieval sage Maimonides whether he could say the words in the prayers, our God and God of our fathers, Maimonides answered yes: Abraham is his father too. And look how the book of Ruth ends. Ruth marries Boaz, and her great-grandson is David, the king. The family line of Israel's king runs through a woman from Moab who chose. Today, people convert within each of the Jewish movements, after study, usually before a rabbinic court, and often with immersion in a ritual bath. The movements differ on the details and on whose conversions they accept, and those differences are real. But the teaching the rabbis left is plain: a person who chose is not a lesser Jew. Fully Jewish.
screen: `GER TZEDEK: A RIGHTEOUS CONVERT.` · `LOVE THE STRANGER AS THYSELF.` · `DON'T BRING UP THEIR PAST.` · `RUTH'S GREAT-GRANDSON, DAVID.` · then, large: `FULLY JEWISH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: welcome someone who chose. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone who joined a group you belong to rather than being born into it: a new neighbor, an in-law, a colleague, someone who came to your faith or your country. Notice whether, somewhere in you, they are still the new one. Then picture saying something that makes it plain they belong, without a word about where they came from. Hold that until the bell, and if you can, say it to them this week. The bell holds the time.
Ger tzedek. A righteous convert, someone who chose to join the Jewish people, and who, like Ruth, is fully Jewish, with a past no one may throw at them. Today's word.

1047.title: Every face
1047.hook: Jews of every color and background
1047.carry: a whole story, not a question
1047.howItsDone: Jewish communities and organizations share the histories of Ethiopian, Indian, Mizrahi, Sephardi, Ashkenazi and other Jews through study, festivals, food and personal stories, and some congregations make a point of welcoming Jews of color and Jews by choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ger tzedek, the Jew by choice, and the line fully Jewish. Did you welcome someone who chose? Today the welcome widens to the whole room. Day one thousand forty-seven.

"And a mixed multitude went up also with them." That's a line from the book of Exodus, about the night the Israelites walked out of Egypt. Not one family. Not one look. A crowd, and the text goes out of its way to say that others walked out with them. Now step into a synagogue on a Saturday morning. The woman handing out prayer books may trace her family to Baghdad. The man beside you, to Addis Ababa, or Kraków, or Kochi, or a small town where nobody else was Jewish. A child in the front row was adopted. Someone at the back chose this people as an adult. Today is about every face in that room.
screen: `A MIXED MULTITUDE.` → `BAGHDAD, ADDIS ABABA, KRAKÓW, KOCHI.` → `EVERY FACE IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, the early collection of rabbinic teaching, asks a strange question. Why did God begin with just one person, one Adam, instead of a whole crowd? It offers several answers. One is so that nobody could ever say to anyone else, my ancestor was greater than yours. Everyone goes back to the same one. Then it reaches for a picture from the mint. When a king stamps coins from one die, every coin comes out the same. God stamped every human being with the seal of the first person, and not one of them is like another. So in this teaching, sameness is the human way of making things. Difference is the divine signature. The prophet Amos says something sharper still. Speaking for God to his own people, he asks: "Are ye not as the children of the Ethiopians unto Me, O children of Israel?" Readers hear the line in more than one way. Some hear a warning against pride: being chosen doesn't put you closer to God than a far-off nation. Others hear it as an embrace that reaches all the way to Africa. Either way, the verse sets Israel and a distant people side by side in God's eyes. The faces of the Jewish people tell that story out loud. Beta Israel from Ethiopia, with their own prayers and the festival of Sigd. The Jews of Cochin in India. Families from Yemen, Iraq, Morocco and Iran. Ashkenazi families from Europe. Jews by choice, and children of every color growing up in Jewish homes. Some Jews of color have described being asked, again and again, are you really Jewish? Yesterday's lesson already answered: someone who belongs, belongs. So today's line is two words, every face. Each face is a whole story, not a question to be checked at the door.
screen: `WHY GOD BEGAN WITH ONE PERSON.` · `ONE SEAL, AND NO TWO COINS ALIKE.` · `AS THE CHILDREN OF THE ETHIOPIANS.` · `A WHOLE STORY BEHIND EACH FACE.` · then, large: `EVERY FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one new story. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a Jewish community you know little about. Ethiopia. India. Yemen. Iran. Or one Jewish person whose family took a road unlike any you know. Hold the questions softly. Where did their grandparents walk? What did they carry? What did they sing on the way? You don't need the answers now. Just make room for them, the way the Mishnah makes room for a face unlike any other. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people of every look who belong. If you don't, simply hold that one community in mind. The bell holds the time.
Every face. The Mishnah's picture: God stamps every person from one seal, and no two come out alike. Today's word.

Your line: a whole story, not a question. Today, when you meet someone new, try trading the question where are you really from for a warmer one: what's your story? Then listen to the whole answer. Day one thousand forty-seven.

1048.title: Cultural Jews
1048.hook: some Jews connect through culture, food, humor and history more than belief
1048.howItsDone: Some Jews express their Jewishness mostly through food, holidays at home, humor, language, books, music and history, and Jewish communities range from Humanistic congregations built on culture and ethics to Orthodox outreach that invites people toward more observance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every face, and your line, a whole story, not a question. Did you learn one new story? Today, a different kind of belonging. Day one thousand forty-eight.

A Friday night kitchen. Someone is braiding challah from a grandmother's recipe, flour up to the elbows. An uncle is telling the same joke he told last year, and everyone groans on cue. A cousin who hasn't set foot in a synagogue in years is arguing hard about a piece of Jewish history. Ask any of them whether they believe in God, and you may get a shrug, a long story, or a laugh. Ask whether they're Jewish, and the answer comes fast: of course. Today is about people who belong through the kitchen, the joke and the story.
screen: `CHALLAH FROM GRANDMOTHER'S RECIPE.` → `THE SAME JOKE AS LAST YEAR.` → `JEWISH? OF COURSE.`

segments.voice: Start with a question the Torah expects to be asked. In Exodus, about the Passover meal, it says: "when your children shall say unto you: What mean ye by this service?" Not if. When. The tradition plans for the person at the table who isn't sure what any of this is for. The Haggadah, the book read at the seder, turns that into four children. One is wise. One is called wicked, because he says this service is for you, not for him. One is simple. And one doesn't even know how to ask. Notice where they all are: at the table. The Haggadah has an answer ready for each one, and for the child who can't ask, it tells the parent to open the conversation. Even the one called wicked gets an answer, a blunt one, and he is still counted among the four. Then there's a line from the Talmud that later rabbis leaned on: an Israelite, even one who has sinned, is still an Israelite. Some teachers read it as a statement about belonging. Being part of this people isn't switched off by doubt. That's why the Hebrew word am, a people, matters so much here. For some Jews, the way in is not a creed. It's Yiddish words in a grandparent's mouth, a pot of soup, a shelf of books, a sense of humor, a history carried in the body. Jewish communities respond to this in different ways. Humanistic Jewish congregations build their whole life around culture, history and ethics. Some Orthodox outreach teachers see the kitchen and the joke as a doorway, and gently invite people further in, toward Shabbat and the commandments. Others stand somewhere in between. Each says what it says. Today's line is simple: culture counts. It's one of the real ways people stay at the table.
screen: `WHAT MEAN YE BY THIS SERVICE?` · `FOUR CHILDREN, ALL AT THE TABLE.` · `STILL AN ISRAELITE.` · `A PEOPLE, NOT ONLY A CREED.` · then, large: `CULTURE COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: honor a cultural connection. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one thing that carries a culture, yours or one you love. A dish. A word only your family uses. A song somebody hummed while cooking. A joke that gets told at every gathering. Hold it the way you'd hold an heirloom. Where did it come from? Who taught it to whom? What would be missing if it stopped being passed on? If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people who carried it to you. If you don't, just say the name of the person who gave it to you. The bell holds the time.
Cultural Jews. Jews who belong through food, humor, language, books and history, sometimes more than through belief. Today's word.
Your line: culture counts. Today, pass one piece of a culture on: a recipe, a word, a story, a song, to someone who hasn't heard it yet. Day one thousand forty-eight.

1049.title: Interfaith families
1049.hook: some Jews live in interfaith families, and communities respond in different ways
1049.howItsDone: Jewish communities respond to interfaith families in different ways: Orthodox and Conservative communities follow descent through the mother and their rabbis generally do not officiate at interfaith weddings, while Reform and Reconstructionist communities accept a child of either Jewish parent raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cultural Jews, and the line culture counts. Did you pass a recipe, a word or a song on to someone? Today, families where two traditions share one table. Day one thousand forty-nine.

A couple sits at a kitchen table with a notebook, planning a wedding. One of them is Jewish. The other isn't. The guest list is easy. The menu is easy. Then come the questions nobody wants to say out loud. Who will marry us? Under a chuppah, or not? And later, quietly: if we have children, what will they be? Their two families are listening from a distance, hoping, worrying, loving them both. Jewish communities have been asked this question for a long time, and they don't all give the same answer.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK AND A WEDDING.` → `WHO WILL MARRY US?` → `WHAT WILL THE CHILDREN BE?`

segments.voice: Begin with the Torah, because it holds more than one view. Moses marries Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro, a priest of Midian. Later, Jethro visits and watches Moses judging the people from morning until evening, alone, worn down. He tells his son-in-law to share the load, and the text says: "So Moses hearkened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said." The great lawgiver takes advice from a priest of another people. But the same Torah also warns against marrying into the nations of Canaan, for fear the children will be turned away from God. And in the book of Ezra, returning exiles are told to send away foreign wives. The Bible doesn't settle this in one verse. The rabbis then made a rule about children: in the Mishnah, a child's Jewish status follows the mother. That rule still shapes communities today, and they respond in different ways. Orthodox communities hold to traditional Jewish law: their rabbis don't officiate at interfaith weddings, and the child of a Jewish mother is Jewish. Conservative communities also follow the mother's line, and some reach out warmly to interfaith families who come through the door. Reform and Reconstructionist communities in North America accept a child with one Jewish parent, mother or father, who is raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate at interfaith weddings while others don't. Each holds its position for reasons it cares about: continuity, law, welcome, love. Meanwhile, real families live it. A non-Jewish parent drives the kids to Hebrew school every week. Grandparents learn new holidays. A child carries two sets of stories. Today's line is honest, and short: families are complex.
screen: `MOSES LISTENS TO JETHRO.` · `THE TORAH ALSO WARNS.` · `STATUS THROUGH THE MOTHER, OR EITHER PARENT.` · `REAL FAMILIES LIVE IT.` · then, large: `FAMILIES ARE COMPLEX.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: welcome one family. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind a family you know that holds more than one tradition. It might be your own. It might be a neighbor's, or a friend's. Picture their table on a holiday. Who feels at home there, and who might feel a little on the edge? Now choose one small welcome you could offer. An invitation. A question asked with real interest: how do you celebrate? Learning the name of one of their holidays. If you pray, you can hold that family in prayer in your own words. If you don't, simply wish them well, one by one. The bell holds the time.
Interfaith families. Households where Jewish and other traditions share one table, met by Jewish communities in different ways. Today's word.
Your line: families are complex. Today, when you hear about someone's family, hold back the quick verdict. Ask one more question, and listen. Day one thousand forty-nine.

1050.title: Jewish humor
1050.hook: laughter as a way of surviving
1050.howItsDone: Jewish humor lives in family stories, folk tales, Yiddish and Ladino sayings, holiday spoofs such as Purim plays, and in writers and comedians, and it is often told by Jews about themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, interfaith families, and the line families are complex. Did you ask one more question before deciding? These last few days have been about who belongs: Jews by choice, every face, cultural Jews, families with two traditions. Today, the week ends with a laugh. Day one thousand fifty.

A man is rescued after years alone on a desert island. His rescuers look around and find he's built himself two synagogues. Why two, they ask. He points. This one I go to. That one, I wouldn't set foot in. People tell that joke at Jewish tables, and they tell it about themselves. It's warm, it's a little sharp, and it's true enough to sting. It also hides something serious. A people that has lived through exile, expulsions and grief kept something in its pocket the whole time: the ability to laugh, including at itself. Today's word is that laughter.
screen: `TWO SYNAGOGUES ON ONE ISLAND.` → `A JOKE TOLD ABOUT OURSELVES.` → `LAUGHTER KEPT IN THE POCKET.`

segments.voice: Laughter shows up early in the Torah, and in an unexpected place. Sarah, old and long past hoping, overhears a visitor tell Abraham she'll have a son. She laughs to herself. When the child is born, she says that God has made laughter for her, and everyone who hears will laugh with her. The boy is named Yitzchak, Isaac, and readers have long heard laughter in that name. So one of the founding families of the people carries a joke in its own name: a promise so unlikely that the only honest answer was to laugh. The Psalms remember laughter at the other end of a hard road. A psalm about coming home from captivity says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter." Not after everything was fixed. At the moment of return, still dusty. And the Talmud tells a small, lovely story. A rabbi named Beroka is standing in a crowded market with the prophet Elijah, and asks him: is anyone here destined for the world to come? Elijah points to two ordinary men. The rabbi goes and asks what they do. They say: we're jesters. When we see someone sad, we cheer them up. When we see two people quarreling, we work to make peace between them. In that whole crowded market, these two are among the very few Elijah points to. That's the root of today's line. In this tradition, humor at its best isn't a way of hiding from pain. It's a way of carrying it, and of carrying each other. A joke can let a frightened room breathe. It can puncture the pompous and spare the weak. It can say, we're still here. Today's line is one word: laugh.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS.` · `THEN WAS OUR MOUTH FILLED WITH LAUGHTER.` · `TWO JESTERS IN THE MARKET.` · `HUMOR THAT CARRIES PAIN.` · then, large: `LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: tell one gentle joke. First, settle and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Now go looking, in memory, for something that made you laugh: a family story, a line a friend said, something a child got gloriously wrong. Choose one that makes nobody smaller. The best ones laugh at life, or at ourselves. Hold it, and notice what it does to your face just to remember it. Then think of one person who could use it today, someone tired, or sad, or in the middle of a quarrel. Like the jesters in the market, you're carrying it to them. The bell holds the time.
Jewish humor. Laughter carried through hard times, aimed at life and at oneself, and honored in the Talmud's story of the two jesters. Today's word.
Your line: laugh. Today, tell that gentle joke to the person who needs it, and laugh with them, not at anyone. Day one thousand fifty.
